clips.title: Alan Parkinson, Creating data for Functional Tests with the Test Data Builder Pattern
clips.why: The problem from the story told by someone who lived it: test data poured into a shared database, and tests that trip over each other.
look: Why SQL scripts that load fixed data become hard to maintain.
What goes wrong when several tests run at once against the same data.
How tests start to depend on rows other tests created.
clips.after: Fixed IDs on QA, such as the collaborator workgroup, are the same trap; the API layer gives each test an empty database instead.

clips.title: Alan Parkinson, Creating data for Functional Tests with the Test Data Builder Pattern
clips.why: The test data builder pattern itself: sensible defaults, and the test names only what it cares about.
look: A builder fills in every value the test does not care about.
The test sets only the values that matter to it, which makes it easier to read.
The builder returns ready-made objects for the test to use.
clips.after: builder.site() and builder.project() do this, with Faker for the defaults.

clips.title: Alan Parkinson, Creating data for Functional Tests with the Test Data Builder Pattern
clips.why: Builders that create objects through the application instead of writing to its database.
look: Creating the data remotely, through the application's own interface.
Why that keeps the data valid by the application's own rules.
clips.after: Our builders call the cloud's API in-process, so the serializer and the permission checks run for every row a test creates.

clips.title: Alan Parkinson, Creating data for Functional Tests with the Test Data Builder Pattern
clips.why: Logical isolation: each test makes unique data, so tests never share or collide.
look: Unique names per test instead of one well-known record.
How unique data lets tests run in parallel.
Isolation without resetting the whole database.
clips.after: Faker's unique emails and slugs give every builder.site() its own workgroup, which pytest-xdist needs.

practice.q: A ported test starts with COLLAB = "65e46694-0951-4634-a839-634af42a8177". What replaces that line?

options.why: A fresh workgroup with its own user, made through the API for this test only.
That keeps the made-up ID and skips the creation path; it is the factory shortcut from the story.
The test needs nothing from QA except data it can build. Skipping it would lose the check.

practice.q: InProcessAPI overrides one method of the QA client. Fill in its name.
practice.hint: The one method that touches the network, with a leading underscore.
practice.why: Every request, including the login, goes through _send, so swapping it changes the transport and nothing else.

practice.q: Django's test client wants headers as META keys. What does the Authorization header become?
practice.hint: HTTP_ plus the name in capitals.
practice.why: Django stores request headers in META with an HTTP_ prefix, dashes as underscores, all in capitals.

practice.q: Put the steps of porting one QA test in order.
items: Copy the test into the API layer with its own calls unchanged
Replace each fixed QA ID with a builder call
Check that it asserts on what a caller sees, not on internal calls
Delete the QA original after two weeks green in CI
practice.why: Move, don't copy: for two weeks both run, and only then is the slow original removed.

practice.q: Why does the dataset builder start the import with sync=False?

options.text: Because asynchronous imports are faster in tests.
options.why: Speed is not the reason. A synchronous import could never finish at all in this setup.

options.text: Because a synchronous import waits in the test's own thread for the client's answer, and the test is the one that must deliver it.
options.why: So the request returns at once, the builder finds the recorded task in the fake and finishes it with complete_task.

options.text: Because the fake client does not support datasets.
options.why: The fake records the scheduled import; the builder finishes it explicitly.

practice.q: A ported test asserts that serializer.save was called once. What is wrong with it?

options.text: Nothing; it proves the endpoint saved the data.
options.why: It proves an internal call happened, and it breaks on a harmless refactoring.

options.text: It checks how the code works instead of what a caller sees; assert on the status code, the fields or the row count instead.
options.why: Tests in the API layer judge behaviour from the outside, so they survive changes inside the code.

options.text: serializer.save cannot be checked in pytest.
options.why: It can be mocked, which is exactly what the new layer avoids.
